title: Around the World in Eighty Days
author: Jules Verne
openingChapterLabel: Chapter 1. In which Phileas Fogg and Passepartout Accept each Other, the One as Master, the Other as Man
openingText: Mr. Phileas Fogg lived, in 1872, at No. 7 Saville Row, Burlington Gardens—the house in which Sheridan had died in 1814. He was one of the most conspicuous members of the Reform Club, though he seemed to do everything he could to avoid attracting attention: an enigmatic figure about whom little was known, except that he was a polished man of the world. People said he resembled Byron—at least his head was Byronic; but he was a bearded, tranquil Byron, the sort who might live a thousand years without growing old.
about:
Phileas Fogg wagers twenty thousand pounds that he can travel around the world in eighty days. That evening he leaves London with his newly hired French servant, Passepartout. Trains, steamships, and carefully calculated connections must bring them back to the Reform Club before the deadline. Delays, dangers, and unexpected encounters keep testing the plan.

Fogg’s composure contrasts with Passepartout’s curiosity and Detective Fix’s suspicions. Their journey becomes both a race against time and a story about what people will risk for one another.

angleCards.title: The plan and the unexpected
angleCards.text: Fogg calculates minutes and connections. Watch how he responds when events refuse to follow the timetable.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the tension between Fogg’s precision and the surprises of the journey.

angleCards.title: Passepartout’s perspective
angleCards.text: Passepartout notices much that his master passes without stopping. His curiosity brings both delight and trouble.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to explore the journey from the servant’s point of view.

angleCards.title: Fix and suspicion
angleCards.text: Fix believes Fogg is a thief. Watch how this conviction shapes his interpretation of Fogg’s actions.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish the evidence Fix sees from the conclusions he draws.

angleCards.title: People before minutes
angleCards.text: Meeting Aouda puts the purpose of the journey in a different light. What matters most when the timetable conflicts with someone else’s need?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the choices in which Fogg risks time and money for others.

cast.name: Phileas Fogg
cast.description: A wealthy Englishman with fixed habits, who reads newspapers and plays whist at the Reform Club. He makes the wager and meets the journey’s difficulties with composure and determination.

cast.name: Passepartout
cast.description: Jean Passepartout has worked as an acrobat, gymnastics teacher, and firefighter. He hopes for a quiet life with Fogg, only to embark immediately on a journey around the world.

cast.name: Fix
cast.description: A British detective who suspects Fogg of the Bank of England theft when he sees him in Suez. He follows him and tries to obtain an arrest warrant.

cast.name: Aouda
cast.description: A young Parsee woman the travellers encounter in India. Her life is in danger, and their attempt to help her shapes the rest of the journey.

cast.name: Sir Francis Cromarty
cast.description: An officer experienced in India who shares part of the journey with Fogg and Passepartout. He helps explain what they encounter and joins the effort to rescue Aouda.

cast.name: The Reform Club
cast.description: The London club where Fogg makes his wager. He must meet his five opponents there again before eighty days have passed.

whyItMatters.title: Suspense by the clock
whyItMatters.body: Departures, delays, and deadlines make even small changes consequential. Readers can follow the running account of hours gained and lost.

whyItMatters.title: Two ways of travelling
whyItMatters.body: Fogg concentrates on the destination while Passepartout attends to what they pass. Their contrast raises questions about what it means to experience the world.

whyItMatters.title: A historical perspective
whyItMatters.body: Steamships, railways, and telegraphs connect the stages of the journey. The narrative also contains colonial assumptions and generalizations about the people the travellers encounter. These form part of the book’s historical perspective.

responses.response: Notice the difference between his calm exterior and his actions. He rarely explains his feelings, but makes choices that cost him money and time. His precision can be read as a habit, a strength, or a way of containing emotion. Consider which interpretation his actions support.

responses.theme: How does the book build suspense?
responses.response: The wager gives the journey a fixed deadline. Every delay changes the chances of catching the next train or ship, and the characters frequently calculate their remaining time. Follow both those calculations and the moments when they must improvise. The narrative’s geographical and historical descriptions should not automatically be treated as verified facts.

responses.theme: What about the book’s colonial assumptions?
responses.response: The narrator describes several groups through generalizations and derogatory language. Notice who speaks and acts as an individual and who becomes scenery or an obstacle. You can follow the adventure while questioning that perspective. Aouda and the Indian guide also deserve attention as people with particular actions, rather than simply stages in Fogg’s journey.

preReadingChat.fallback: We can discuss Fogg’s habits, Passepartout’s curiosity, Fix’s suspicion, or the way the timetable generates suspense. Which thread would you like to follow?
